messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kai stood at the stainless-steel counter of the diner’s prep station, his knife moving through a pile of onions with mechanical precision. He could tell the story of what happened that night without hesitating—he had told it to the police, to his ex-wife, to the therapist he saw twice before quitting—but the order of events never held together in his mind. One moment he was wiping down the pass after the dinner rush, the sous chef clapping him on the shoulder in congratulations. The next, he was on the floor of the dry storage room, the smell of garlic and sweat thick in his nostrils, and he was pushing, pushing, but his body would not cooperate. He could not remember how he got from the pass to the floor, or whether the overhead light was on or off. The middle was a dark gap that he had never been able to fill. And when he tried to hold the whole thing in his head, something inside him would slam a door shut, and he would find himself staring at the onions again, the blade moving, his mind blank.

Kai was forty-five, a chef for twenty-two years, and he had always known himself through his hands—the way he could season a broth by instinct, the way a perfect sear felt under his spatula. That was what he was, what he had been. But since the rape, two years ago now, something had curdled. He felt dirty all the time, a greasy film on his skin that no shower could rinse away. When he walked into the diner kitchen each morning, the heat and the clatter of pans felt like an accusation. He was certain that the other line cooks could smell it on him, that they knew what had been done to him, that they saw a man who could be taken apart so easily. He had stopped accepting the evening shift because the dimmer lighting and the smaller crew made his chest seize, and he had stopped working saucier because the garlic-heavy broths brought the taste of that night back into his throat. He took the morning biscuit station instead, safest and most anonymous, and he told the owner it was because his back bothered him.

His marriage had not survived the year that followed. His wife had tried to understand, but Kai could not let her touch him without flinching. He had come to believe that something inside him was irreparably spoiled, that any intimacy would only spread the contamination. She left, and he had nodded because it felt like the natural conclusion. His life had been destroyed—he was certain of that now, the way he was certain of the recipe for hollandaise. The destruction was not dramatic; it was the slow erosion of everything that had made him feel like himself. He no longer experimented with dishes. He no longer took pride in plating. He went to work, he chopped, he went home, he watched television until his eyes burned, and then he did it again.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a Thursday morning when he could not bring himself to open the walk-in cooler. The handle was cold, the light inside was flickering, and the confined space smelled of raw protein and bleach. His legs would not move. He stood in the hallway for ten minutes until a dishwasher asked if he was okay, and then he called in sick and drove straight to the intake office. He was not sure what he hoped for—maybe that someone could help him put the order of events back together, or that they could tell him how to feel clean again. More than anything, he wanted to believe that the man he used to be was still in there somewhere, buried under the grime of what had happened, and that it was not too late to scrub him out.
